750.title: Peter and Paul in Rome
750.hook: after Nero's fire, tradition says Peter was crucified upside down and Paul beheaded
750.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches keep a shared feast of Saints Peter and Paul, and pilgrims visit the churches in Rome built over the places tradition names as their graves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's journeys, and your line was he made tents. What ordinary work did you do as part of something bigger? Today the road ends in Rome. Day seven hundred fifty.

The book of Acts stops in a strange place. Paul has reached Rome as a prisoner, after a storm and a shipwreck, and the last lines in the King James Bible say: "And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him." He is teaching, the very last words say, "no man forbidding him." And then the book simply ends. No verdict. No execution. Peter dropped out of the story long before. For what happened next to both men, the churches turned to tradition, and in that tradition the story runs through a fire.

The Roman historian Tacitus writes that after a great fire burned through Rome, the emperor Nero blamed the Christians, and had them put to death in cruel ways. Tradition places Peter and Paul in Rome in those years, and it remembers their deaths. Peter, it says, was crucified, and asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die the way his Lord had. Paul, a Roman citizen, was beheaded with the sword. The New Testament doesn't tell either death. But it leaves two signs. In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus tells Peter, the one who had denied him by the fire: "when thou shalt be old, thou shalt stretch forth thy hands, and another shall gird thee, and carry thee whither thou wouldest not." And John adds: "This spake he, signifying by what death he should glorify God." Then Jesus says two words: "Follow me." The man who once said "I know not the man" is told he'll follow all the way. The second sign is a letter in Paul's name, written from prison to Timothy: "I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Not I have won. Not I was right. I have kept the faith. Two very different men. The fisherman who sank in the water and the tentmaker who once made havoc of the church. They argued once, in Antioch, face to face. And Christian tradition remembers them together, buried in the same city, honored on the same feast. Catholic tradition places Peter's grave beneath the church that bears his name in Rome. Whatever you make of the traditions, both stories come to the same place: faithful to the end.

Here's the practice: honor someone who paid for their conscience. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person, from any time or any faith or none, who refused to say what they didn't believe, and lost something for it: a job, their freedom, their life. It can be someone famous, or someone in your own family. Hold their face, or their name. Think about what it cost, and what they kept. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for them. If you don't, simply honor them in silence. The bell holds the time.
Nero. The emperor under whom tradition remembers both Peter and Paul dying in Rome, honored together by the churches.
Your line: faithful to the end. Today, finish one thing you promised, even a small one, all the way to the end. Day seven hundred fifty.

751.title: The temple falls (AD 70)
751.hook: Rome destroys the temple, and both Judaism and Christianity must learn to live without it
751.carry: pray for the peace of jerusalem
751.howItsDone: Christians pray for Jerusalem with the words of Psalm 122, and the fall of the temple is read in churches from the Gospels, where Jesus foretells it and weeps over the city.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nero, and your line was faithful to the end. What did you finish? Today, a loss that changed two faiths at once. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

Walking out of the temple in Jerusalem, the rebuilt temple that stood where the old one had burned, a disciple turns to Jesus, full of awe: "Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!" Look at the size of these stones. And Jesus answers: "Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down." In Mark's Gospel, it's said in passing, on the way out. Years later, Roman armies put down a revolt in Judaea, and the temple burns. The house of God in Jerusalem is gone. Jews and Christians both have to answer the same question: now what?

Start with grief, because the texts do. Luke says that when Jesus came near the city, "he beheld the city, and wept over it." He wept for Jerusalem, not against it. The temple was the center of Jewish worship: sacrifice, the festivals, the priests. For the first Christians, it was their temple too; Acts shows the apostles praying there day after day. When it fell, both communities had to find how God is worshiped without it. Jewish tradition tells of teachers who rebuilt Judaism around prayer, study and the home. A rabbinic story remembers a teacher walking past the ruins with a student who mourns that the place of atonement is gone. The teacher says there is another atonement as good: deeds of loving-kindness, and he quotes the prophet Hosea: "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice." Christians know that verse too. In Matthew, Jesus quotes it twice. Jews still mourn the temple on a fast day, Tisha B'Av, and at a Jewish wedding, tradition breaks a glass to remember Jerusalem in the middle of joy. Christians, for their part, spoke of a temple that couldn't burn. John says that when Jesus said destroy this temple, "he spake of the temple of his body." And Paul writes to Corinth: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" Two faiths, one loss, and some shared verses to carry it. And the city itself is still prayed for, in a psalm both Jews and Christians sing: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee."

Here's the practice: pray, or hope, for Jerusalem. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the city as it is today: Jews at the Western Wall, Christians in the old churches, Muslims at their mosque, families in ordinary streets, people who are afraid. Don't take a side for two minutes. Just hold all of them. If you pray, you can say the psalm's own line slowly, a few times: pray for the peace of Jerusalem. If you don't pray, hold the city in your attention and wish it peace. The bell holds the time.
Tisha B'Av. The fast day when Jews still mourn the temple Rome destroyed in Jerusalem, a loss that taught both Jews and Christians to worship without it.
Your line: pray for the peace of jerusalem. Today, when you see a headline about the city, stop for one breath and wish it peace before you scroll on. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

752.title: The gospels written down
752.hook: as eyewitnesses aged, their memories were written as the four gospels
752.howItsDone: Churches read from the Gospels in their services, often standing for the reading, and in several churches the reading plan moves through Matthew, Mark and Luke over a cycle of years, with John read at special seasons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tisha B'Av, and your line was pray for the peace of jerusalem. Did you stop for a breath before scrolling on? Today, what the church did with its memories. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

Who in your family still remembers the oldest stories? The grandmother who knows how your great-grandparents met. The uncle who was there when the house burned. A lot of families have someone like that, and sooner or later somebody says: we should write this down. The early church had that moment too. The people who had walked with Jesus wouldn't be there forever. A letter in Peter's name says it plainly: "I will endeavour that ye may be able after my decease to have these things always in remembrance." The stories were still told aloud, at tables and in prayers, but the voices were thinning. Today is about the decision to put the memories on paper, and what one writer says about why.

Luke opens his Gospel like a careful historian, and in the King James Bible it reads: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us, Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word." Notice what he admits. He isn't the first to try. Others have written already. And the stories came from eyewitnesses who delivered them, handed them on, the way tradition works. Luke says he's going to write it "in order," so that his friend Theophilus might "know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed." Mark starts with no introduction at all: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." Straight in. An early tradition, preserved by the church historian Eusebius, says Mark wrote down what Peter remembered. John ends with a confession: there's far more than this. "And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book: But these are written, that ye might believe." And at the very end, almost with a smile: if everything were written down, "even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written." So the church ended up with four Gospels, under the names tradition gives them: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. They tell the same Jesus from four angles, and they don't always line up in detail. In the end the churches kept all four side by side instead of blending them into one. Four accounts, each in its own voice, written down before they forget.
screen: `THESE ARE WRITTEN, THAT YE MIGHT BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write down one story from an elder. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone older who told you a story more than once: a parent, a grandparent, a neighbor, a teacher. Let one story come back. Where were they? Who was there? What did they say at the end? Then, if you have something to write with, put it down in a few lines, plain, the way they told it. Don't polish it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the person who told it. The bell holds the time.
Luke. The evangelist who wrote his gospel in order, so Theophilus might know the certainty of what he'd been taught, as the church set its eyewitness memories on paper.
Your line: before they forget. Today, ask one older person to tell you a story you've never heard, and write it down. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

753.title: The Didache: two ways
753.hook: an early handbook: there are two ways, of life and of death; pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day
753.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the Lord's Prayer at set times through the day, and churches that pray morning and evening prayer include it in each service; the Didache is read today as an early Christian writing, not as scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke, and your line was before they forget. Whose story did you write down? Today, a book written for the people learning those stories. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

A short book, only a handful of pages, and it isn't in the Bible. It's something more like a church's handbook: what to teach new believers, how to baptize, when to fast, how to pray, what to do with traveling preachers. Its title calls it the teaching of the twelve apostles. It's very practical. If a traveling apostle stays more than a couple of days, or asks for money, the book says, he's a false prophet. Somebody had clearly met that guy. But the book doesn't open with rules. It opens with a choice.

The word is Didache, Greek for teaching, and its first line says there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and a great difference between them. The picture isn't new. Moses says it in Deuteronomy: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Jeremiah says it too: "Behold, I set before you the way of life, and the way of death." Jews and Christians share the image. Then the Didache describes the way of life, and it sounds like the Sermon on the Mount turned into a checklist for beginners. Love God who made you. Love your neighbor as yourself. Whatever you wouldn't want done to you, don't do to another. Bless those who curse you. Pray for your enemies. Give to everyone who asks. The way of death is the list of what breaks people: lies, greed, cruelty, pride. Later, the handbook turns to prayer. It gives the Lord's Prayer, the one from Matthew's Gospel that begins "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name," with a short line of praise at the end, and then a plain instruction: pray it three times a day. Not a new prayer. The same one, three times over, so that the day has a shape. The Didache isn't part of the Bible. But it's a window into how some early Christians tried to live: two ways, and a prayer said again and again to stay on one of them.
screen: `THE LORD'S PRAYER, THREE TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the first of three. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say the Lord's Prayer once now, slowly, one line per breath, and let each line land before the next. Then decide when the other two will be today: midday, maybe, and before sleep. If you don't pray, read or recall the prayer's lines slowly as words, and notice which line catches. Either way, set two small reminders for later. The handbook's idea is simple: the same words, three times, give a day its shape. The bell holds the time.
Didache. Greek for teaching. An early Christian handbook that opens with two ways, of life and of death, and asks for the Lord's Prayer three times a day.
Your line: two ways. Today, at one small choice, ask which way leads to life, and take that one. Then keep your two reminders. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

754.title: Clement of Rome
754.hook: a letter from Rome to quarreling Corinth: be humble, be at peace
754.howItsDone: Clement's letter is read today among the writings of the Apostolic Fathers, and the Catholic Church remembers Clement as a saint and an early bishop of Rome.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Didache, and your line was two ways. Did you keep your reminders to pray, or pause? Today, a church that chose the wrong way, and a letter that tried to turn it. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

The church in Corinth has pushed out its leaders. Not for stealing, not for false teaching. A few bold people stirred things up, and the elders who had served well were removed. The news travels across the sea to the church in Rome, and Rome writes back: a long letter, patient and firm, from one church to another. It opens with a greeting from the church of God sojourning at Rome to the church sojourning at Corinth. It never signs a personal name. But tradition names the one who held the pen: Clement, a leader of the Roman church. And Corinth, it turns out, had been here before.

Clement reminds them: take up the letter of the blessed Paul. Years earlier Paul had written to this same church about the same problem. In the King James Bible: "every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ." Different camps, same quarrel. Clement's medicine is humility. He quotes the old proverb that also appears in the Letter of James: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." He fills page after page with examples from the scriptures of people who were lowly and were lifted up, and of jealousy that destroyed people, from Cain onward. He reaches for Peter and Paul too, as examples from his own generation, who suffered through jealousy and strife. Then he writes a hymn to love, close to Paul's own: love makes no divisions, love stirs up no rebellion, love does all things in harmony. And then he asks something remarkable of the people who started the trouble. Whoever is noble among you, he writes, let him say: if this fight is because of me, I'll leave; I'll go wherever you want; only let the flock of Christ be at peace with its elders. Not throw them out. Invite them to step down on their own. Paul had told the Philippians the same: "in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves." Catholic tradition counts Clement among the early bishops of Rome. The letter's message, for Corinth: let the proud be humbled, and let the flock be at peace.
screen: `I AM OF PAUL; AND I OF APOLLOS.`
`IF IT'S BECAUSE OF ME, I'LL GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: draft a peacemaking note. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one strained relationship: a friend, a sibling, a coworker, someone in a group you belong to. Ask Clement's hard question, quietly: how much of this is because of me? Don't argue the other side's case for them. Just look at yours. Then, in your head or on your phone, write three plain sentences to that person. No blame. Just your own share of it, named plainly. You don't have to send it yet. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. The bell holds the time.
Clement. The leader tradition names as the writer of the Roman church's letter to quarreling Corinth: be humble, and be at peace.
Your line: let the proud be humbled. Today, in one disagreement, be the first to give a little ground, and see what happens. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

755.title: Ignatius on the road
755.hook: chained on his way to the lions, he writes that he is God's wheat (Romans 4)
755.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches remember Ignatius of Antioch as a saint and martyr, and his letters are read today among the writings of the Apostolic Fathers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clement, and your line was let the proud be humbled. Did you give a little ground somewhere? Today, another letter headed for Rome, written in chains. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

A prisoner is being marched overland toward Rome, chained to a squad of soldiers. He calls them ten leopards, and says they only get worse when they're treated kindly. He is Ignatius, and in his letters he calls himself the bishop of Syria; tradition places his church in Antioch. He is going to Rome to die in the arena. Along the road, Christians come out to meet him in the towns he passes, and he writes letters to their churches. One letter goes ahead of him, to the Christians in Rome. It's a strange letter. It's a request. Please, don't save me.

Ignatius worries that the Roman Christians will try to step in. So he writes, in effect: say nothing on my behalf. Let me go. Then comes the picture that gives today its line. I am God's wheat, he writes, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found pure bread of Christ. It's a startling thing to say about your own death. Wheat is not finished when it's harvested. It has to be ground before it can feed anyone. Some readers hear an echo of words Jesus says in John's Gospel: "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." And for Christians who share bread at the Lord's table, the picture of becoming bread is hard to miss. Readers hear this letter in different ways. Some are moved by a man so sure of Christ that he walks toward the arena without flinching. Some are uneasy, and ask whether he wanted death too much. Both reactions take the letter seriously. And notice the rest of the road. A condemned man, with every reason to think only of himself, spends his last journey writing to other people's churches: be united, gather together often, care for the widows, be patient with one another. He is already being ground into bread, letter by letter, for people he would never see again.

Here's the practice: think of your life as bread for others. Settle, and breathe. Bread is ordinary. It gets broken, shared, eaten, gone. Bring to mind the people who are fed, in some way, by your days: the ones you cook for, work for, listen to, look after. Picture each one for a breath. Then ask: what in me is being ground down right now, and could it become something that feeds someone? Tiredness, patience, time. If you pray, you can offer your day to God as bread. If you don't, simply hold the people who depend on you. The bell holds the time.
Ignatius. A bishop chained on the way to Rome, writing to churches as he goes, and asking the Romans to let him become God's wheat.
Your line: god's wheat. Today, at the moment you feel ground down, do one small thing that feeds someone else. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

756.title: Polycarp
756.hook: asked to curse Christ, the old bishop says he's served him eighty-six years and he's done no wrong
756.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches remember Polycarp as a saint and martyr on his feast day, and the Martyrdom of Polycarp is read as an early example of Christians keeping the anniversary of a martyr's death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius, and your line was god's wheat. What did you do for someone while you felt ground down? Today, an old man who had read Ignatius's letters. Day seven hundred fifty-six.

Soldiers arrive at a farmhouse outside Smyrna late in the evening. The man they've come for could have run again. He doesn't. He comes downstairs, talks with them, and, according to the account written by his church, orders food and drink set out for them, as much as they want. Then he asks one thing: time to pray. They give it, and he prays so long, and so fully, that some of the men who came to arrest him are sorry they came. His name is Polycarp. He is the bishop of Smyrna, and he is very old. Before long he'll be standing in the stadium.

The Martyrdom of Polycarp is a letter from his church, telling what happened. In the stadium the crowd is roaring. The Roman governor, the proconsul, is almost gentle. Have respect for your age, he says. Swear by the fortune of Caesar. Say: away with the atheists. That's what the crowd called Christians, because they wouldn't honor the gods. Polycarp looks up at the packed stands, waves his hand at the crowd, groans, looks to heaven, and says: away with the atheists. He says the words, and turns them around. The governor presses. Swear, and I'll let you go. Curse Christ. And Polycarp answers, in the line the church remembered: eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me? Some readers take eighty-six years as his age, others as the years since his baptism. Either way, it's a lifetime. The governor threatens wild beasts, then fire. Polycarp answers that the governor's fire burns for a little while and goes out. The account says the fire was lit around him, and in the end an executioner's dagger took his life. And then a very human detail: afterward his church gathered his bones and laid them somewhere safe, and planned to gather there to keep the day of his death as a birthday. Tradition says Polycarp had known John, the disciple of Jesus. That ties him to the story we've walked this week: Peter and Paul, Luke, the Didache, Clement's plea, Ignatius. Polycarp had even received a letter from Ignatius himself.

Here's the practice: name a long faithfulness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've been faithful to for years: a spouse, a friend, a parent, a child, a congregation, a promise. Count the years, roughly. Notice what those years held: the good, the dull, the hard. Then turn it around: who has been faithful to you for years? Hold both names. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for them, and for whatever has kept you faithful. If you don't, simply let gratitude sit with you. The bell holds the time.
